_comment: Ledger of recurring prose habits (constructions, gestures, paragraph/scene closers), the language-level counterpart to motifs.json. Nightly sessions read this before drafting and add entries after. Status: 'develop' = use only in a new form; 'rest' = do not use until rested_until chapter; 'watch' = fine in moderation. Saturday review prunes and logs counts.

constructions.pattern: 'the way [clause]' used as a trailing simile
constructions.example: the way you feel an old break in the weather before you feel the ache of it
constructions.note: Zero again in ch. 16, a delirium chapter built almost entirely out of manner-clause comparisons (the stairs, the voices, the courteous man) that was drafted with several 'the way X' constructions and had every one of them rewritten to a plain 'as' clause or cut, same remedy as ch. 15. Demoting to rest as flagged last time — five of the last six chapters at zero or one. Leave this construction alone for a real stretch; the plain-'as' replacement is doing the work now. Ch. 17 (first Maria chapter, new POV) drafted with nine instances of this exact shape on a first pass and every one was rewritten to a plain 'as' clause before the chapter was finished — the rest period holds even under a brand-new narrating voice; don't let POV novelty be an excuse to re-open it early. Ch. 18's first pass produced two more ('the room filled up with newsprint the way it had filled...', 'filed under history... the way the Attrition had become...') and both were rewritten, one to 'exactly as', one restructured entirely. Two chapters from the rest lifting, the pull toward this shape is still there every time; keep rewriting it out rather than assuming the habit is gone. Ch. 19's first pass produced the heaviest pull yet — eight separate instances across all four sections ('opened it the way other people say grace', 'the bad arm held the way a man holds a tool he trusts', 'the way he'd have told me the kettle had boiled', and five more) plus a 'the same way' variant, every one caught and rewritten to a plain 'as' clause, a flat declarative, or a restructured sentence before the chapter was finished. One chapter left on the rest clock; the habit shows no sign of weakening on its own, so the rewrite-on-sight discipline is doing all the work, not time.

constructions.example: a thing to explain; a thing your body has quietly decided
constructions.note: Seventh chapter running at zero, including ch. 16, where a vague placeholder noun would have been the easy way to gesture at everything delirium left unnamed and wasn't reached for even once. Safe to consider this one fully retired rather than merely resting. Eighth clean chapter now in ch. 17 — a first draft used 'a thing' twice (Maria's new voice reaching for the same vague filler) and both were replaced with 'something' or cut. Treat as fully retired across POVs, not just Lloyd's. Ninth clean chapter in ch. 18 — a first draft used it twice more ('not a thing she said', 'hiding a thing from me') and both were rephrased ('that sort of thing', 'anything'). Fully retired; stop flagging unless it reappears. It reappears in ch. 19, twice, but in a different shape worth distinguishing from the retired filler: 'what a thing was worth' and 'what the Church meant when it called a thing settled' both use 'a thing' as a specific, load-bearing noun echoing the chapter's own title, not a vague placeholder standing in for something unnamed. Left in deliberately rather than cut. Keep watching for the vague-filler version returning, but don't flag this title-echo usage as a lapse.

constructions.pattern: 'I have learned/found/never...' followed by a general rule
constructions.example: I have learned the exact weight a thing has to reach before it's worth the cost of saying it out loud
constructions.note: Seventh chapter running at zero. A draft pass of ch. 16 produced a near-miss ('is, I have come to understand, a different skill altogether') in the Ivet beat and it was cut back to a plain statement with no self-aware hedge. Stays on watch rather than retired, since the delirium register makes this one easy to slip back into. Ch. 17 (Maria, new POV) stayed clean of the general-rule shape, but see the new 'i-have-anaphora' entry below — her confessional voice reaches for 'I have [verb]' sentence openers constantly, and this aphorism pattern is the thing that habit could calcify into if a later chapter lets one of those openers run on into a stated general rule instead of a flat personal fact. Ch. 18 stayed clean too, and went further than clean: the chapter drops 'I have' openers to zero entirely (see i-have-anaphora) rather than letting one calcify into this pattern, though a few present-tense generalizations slipped in elsewhere ('there is nothing left over to accuse') as flat institutional observation rather than self-aware personal rule — different enough in register to leave off this ledger, but worth a glance next time. Ch. 19 stays clean again, and the Edie ledger scene offered an obvious opening ('I have learned that a thing's worth and its cost are never the same question') that was written instead as two flat declaratives with no stated rule attached. Tenth clean chapter.

Ch. 16 at 19, same band held through a whole-chapter unreliable-narration experiment. Contrast partner rotated to its most minimal form yet: Lloyd's long, overlapping delirium sentences pulled up short by Maria's bare grounding words reaching him from outside the slide (cup. window. blanket. her own hand.) rather than by another character's combat calls or institutional paperwork. Ch. 17 (first Maria chapter) holds the same band at 22, and did rotate the contrast partner as flagged: her long, looping guilt-sentences get cut short by plain nursing fact ('I did that.' 'I have checked.') rather than by anyone's dialogue. Keep watching that the short side doesn't collapse into the new i-have-anaphora habit below instead of staying genuinely varied. Ch. 18 drops to 14 — a real dip, not noise — because the chapter leans on short declarative dialogue (Lloyd and Edie both terse by canon) and bureaucratic one-liners ('Nobody senior was charged.') as its contrast partner instead of another long sentence immediately following. Worth deciding whether 18-22 or occasional dips into the mid-teens is the real band for Maria's voice before flagging a trend either way. Ch. 19 climbs back to 21, closer to the 17/18 pre-dip high than the ch. 18 low, with a third contrast partner this time: Edie's ledger lines and one-word exchanges ('Good.' 'Work.' 'Said if.') cutting against Maria's looping sums. The 18-22 band looks like the real one; ch. 18's 14 reads as the outlier, tied to that chapter's unusually dialogue-light newsprint sections, rather than the start of a downward trend.

constructions.pattern: 'same as [clause]' used as a trailing comparison, the direct replacement for the rested the-way-simile
constructions.example: same as I run all of them back now
constructions.note: Four chapters running at exactly one use (Maria's hand on his chest, 'the same as I had every single time since the chapel'). Settled, controlled background usage. Ch. 17 drops to zero — the first chapter not to reach for it at all — likely just the new POV finding its own shapes rather than a deliberate rest; worth checking whether it resumes at one in ch. 18 before reading anything into the dip. It resumed in ch. 18, at two rather than one ('same as she always did', 'same as I set down anything I can't carry') — both load-bearing rather than decorative, but worth holding at one going forward rather than letting it creep upward now that it's also absorbing some of the retired the-way-simile's old work. Ch. 19 held at exactly one as instructed ('same as he asked anything he already half expected would go unanswered', Lloyd asking what's in Carrowgate) — a second natural opening (the gaslamps, 'punctual regardless') was deliberately rewritten without the construction to keep the count down. The one-per-chapter discipline is holding.

constructions.pattern: Lloyd narrates his own perception-management in filing/accounting/procedural language
constructions.example: filed and closed and not brought up again; I did the sum; running the frame back
constructions.note: Sixth chapter running clean. Ch. 16 was the strongest possible temptation for this one — a whole chapter of Lloyd trying to manage facts he can't otherwise process, including the knot-cord count — and it still reached for arithmetic as a dry joke rather than filing language. Treat as effectively retired. Ch. 16 was also Lloyd's last chapter on the page for the whole of Act III: the POV has moved to Maria for ch. 17-25, and since this construction is defined around Lloyd's specific filing-and-accounting self-talk, it's dormant rather than tracked for the Maria chapters — pick it back up only if the narration returns to Lloyd.

constructions.pattern: a clause restated through its own negation for flat understatement — 'didn't X because there wasn't X to do', 'wasn't an answer that wasn't Y'
constructions.example: she didn't say anything useful, because there wasn't anything useful to say; I didn't have an answer that wasn't the same thing said back to her, worse
constructions.note: Sixth chapter running without it. Not reached for in ch. 16 either, despite several places (the buried memory, the cord) where a negated restatement would have been an easy shape to default to; still safe to use if it arises naturally, not a default. Seventh clean chapter in ch. 17, carrying the habit's absence across the Act III POV change. Eighth clean chapter in ch. 18, including the letter scene, which had an obvious opening for it ('there wasn't a threat that wasn't...') and used a plainer construction instead ('There was no threat folded anywhere inside it'). Ninth clean chapter in ch. 19 — the farewell scene's 'not her fare, not a hand with the bag, not so much as a kind word' runs on repeated plain negation instead, a different and so far untracked anaphoric shape, not this one.

constructions.pattern: a statement capped with a trailing 'which was/is [flat judgment]' clause
constructions.example: which was true, and also the kindest thing she could have said to her just then; which was as much of a question as Edie generally asks
constructions.note: Four chapters clean now. A draft pass of ch. 16's opening produced one bare trailing 'which told me...' close and it was split into two short declaratives instead, same remedy as ch. 12-13. Treat any return to the bare trailing-'which' shape as a real lapse. Ch. 17's first draft produced two more (Edie's visit, the prayer paragraph) and both were split into separate declarative sentences before the chapter was finished, same remedy again — this is clearly the construction Maria's looping, qualifying sentences most want to fall into, so keep watching every chapter of hers for it, not just occasionally. Ch. 18's first draft produced five more (Lloyd's silence, the carrying metaphor, the landlady's tact, Edie leaving the letter, the library shelving), every one split into separate sentences before the chapter was finished — the highest single-draft count yet for this construction, in a chapter built almost entirely out of exactly the explanatory-aside material ('she did X, which meant Y') this pattern feeds on. Treat this as the construction most likely to reappear unedited in a rushed draft; it is being caught, not avoided by instinct. Ch. 19's first draft produced one more, in the ledger scene ('she had only ever cared what it cost, which I had slowly come to understand were not the same question at all, and that she was the only one... who had never once confused them') — split into three short declaratives before the chapter was finished. Still being caught every single chapter; five chapters running in a row now where a draft pass reaches for this shape at least once.

constructions.pattern: a short sentence opens with 'I have [verb]' as a flat, ledger-like confessional statement — a new habit, first seen in Maria's own first-person voice
constructions.example: I have checked. I have turned the arithmetic of that every way it will go. I have tried the sentence several ways and none of them let me off.
constructions.note: New in ch. 17, Maria's first chapter as narrator — five instances, all in the two interior reckoning paragraphs (the prayer, the Vail wound, the register). Distinct from the retired i-have-learned-aphorism: no general rule gets stated, each one is a flat personal fact standing on its own, closer to a confession she's logging than an observation about how the world works. Reads as earned characterisation right now — her guilt literalised as bookkeeping — but five in one chapter is enough to flag. Watch ch. 18-19 for whether it keeps recurring at this rate; if so, it wants evolving (vary the opener, or let a later chapter withhold it deliberately) rather than repeating as a default confessional tic. Ch. 18 drops it to zero outright — deliberately withheld, per the note above, since her attention this chapter is on the newspapers and the institution rather than her own private ledger. But see the i-had-anaphora entry below: the same confessional impulse resurfaced in the past-perfect instead of the present-perfect, which is evolution in tense only, not in kind. Don't credit ch. 18 with having retired the habit; it relocated. Ch. 19 holds at zero again, and this time i-had-anaphora also drops to zero — see below for the fronting technique that did it.

constructions.pattern: a sentence opens with 'I had [verb]' as a flat retrospective anaphora — the past-perfect cousin of i-have-anaphora, used the chapter that habit was deliberately withheld
constructions.example: I had read Anse Duley's name in it most nights for six weeks. I had not decided, until Edie's hand was actually out for it, whether I could put it in that hand.
constructions.note: New in ch. 18. Seven instances, spread across all three sections rather than clustered in one reckoning paragraph the way i-have-anaphora was in ch. 17 — this version reads more like a structural habit of hers than a confined confessional outburst, which may make it harder to notice and easier to let calcify. Watch ch. 19-20 for whether Maria's narration keeps reaching for 'I had' as a default sentence opener regardless of which present-perfect or past-perfect variant is in use; if both keep recurring under different tenses, the real habit is the anaphoric 'I have/had [verb]' opener itself, and it may be worth merging these two entries and evolving the shape rather than tracking the tenses separately. Ch. 19's first draft had five sentence-initial 'I had [verb]' openers; every one was rewritten before the chapter was finished, mostly by moving an adverbial phrase ('Three days before,', 'Slowly,') to the front of the sentence so the clause lands mid-sentence instead of as the opener, keeping the underlying fact. Final count zero for both variants, confirming the real habit is the sentence-initial position itself rather than either tense. Recommend merging these two entries next review into one 'i-have/had-anaphora' entry tracking opener position across both tenses, and keep using the adverbial-fronting fix going forward.

closers.pattern: paragraph or chapter ends on the narrator stating what he did not say, or what the scene means
closers.example: I said none of that. I hadn't said anything since the school wall and didn't start now.
closers.note: Ch. 15 and ch. 16 both avoid it. Ch. 16 ends on a bare image — daylight through the gap in the Callow Ford roof, mid-slide, no resolving line and nothing stated about what it means — which is the chapter's own outline requirement (no lucid interval, no final clarity) as much as it is this ledger's preference. Three chapters (12-14) still the longest run on this pattern; neither ch. 15 nor ch. 16 is added to the chapters list. Ch. 17 also avoids it: ends on Maria's hand on Lloyd's chest and the plain fact of feeling him believe her, not on any statement of what the moment meant. Four chapters clean running into Act III. Ch. 18 keeps the streak: ends on the letter folded away into the floorboard gap the register left, a plain action on a plain object, with no line stating what keeping-and-not-answering it means. Five chapters clean. Ch. 19 keeps it going: ends on Edie's footsteps fading down the stair and the paper still in Maria's hand, nothing stated about what the realisation (that Edie never once asked them for anything) means or costs — the realisation itself is shown as the outline's own beat, landed through what Edie didn't do, not through the narrator glossing it afterward. Six chapters clean.

closers.pattern: chapter ends on an image of something indifferent or inanimate personified as 'patient', waiting out time without hurry
closers.example: the night came down slow over the burnt manse... patient, working at the dark the way it works at everything, given enough time and no one to tell it to stop
closers.note: Spent at ch. 08-09 review; stayed spent through ch. 13. Do not return to 'patient' as a chapter-ending word.
